explanations.answer: Turn in your account since you can't stay manager
explanations.explanation: The rich man skips the warning and goes straight to the verdict: "Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) That's not a talk, friend. That's the apron coming off. Hand in the books, and the job is over.

explanations.answer: Pay back every coin by tomorrow
explanations.explanation: No deadline, no coins, no repayment plan. The rich man tells him, "Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) He wants the books, and the job is done. Honestly, if somebody gave me until TOMORROW to fix my crooked years, I'd still be behind the takeout menus.

explanations.answer: Work for free until it's fixed
explanations.explanation: Work for free? Friend, nobody in this story gets a second shift. The rich man says, "Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) Hand in the account, and that's the end of it. No unpaid overtime to bake his way back in.

He says the exact opposite! Listen to him: "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) Digging's out. Begging's out. Both backup plans hit the floor before he finishes the sentence, like me dropping a whole tray on the way to the oven.

You caught it. The manager crosses off both options himself: "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) That's a man scrolling job listings going nope. Nope. NOPE. With both doors shut, he's going to need a brand new plan.

Homes it is! The manager says, "I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) The job's going away, so he's thinking about who'll still open the door for him. He's the coworker passing out cookies his last week so everybody keeps inviting him over.

Palaces? Friend, this man is aiming way lower than that. His plan is that "people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) Regular homes. He's not dreaming about a throne. He just hopes somebody still answers when he knocks.

No tents in this plan, baker. The manager says "people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) Homes! He's not planning a camping trip after he loses the job. He wants a couch and a door that opens.

explanations.answer: A hundred measures of olive oil
explanations.explanation: Olive oil, a hundred measures of it! "A hundred measures of olive oil," he answered. (Luke 16:6) That's no little tab at the corner store, friend. That's a BIG number owed to one master, and the manager is about to do something with it.

Barley's a grain, and it's not on this man's bill. "A hundred measures of olive oil," he answered. (Luke 16:6) Grain does show up, though! The very next debtor owes a hundred measures of wheat (Luke 16:7), so you were just one bill early.
No honey on this bill, friend. "A hundred measures of olive oil," he answered. (Luke 16:6) Oil, a hundred measures of it. That's a big debt to one master, and the manager is about to start writing.

FIFTY! The manager says, "Take your bill," and then, "sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) A hundred measures of olive oil cut in half, faster than my oven timer can beep. I have never split a batch that fast, and I've been trying for years.

Two hundred would double the bill, and the manager goes the other way! He tells the debtor to "sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) A hundred down to fifty. If somebody offered to chop my tab in half, I'd sit down quickly too.

Three hundred? Friend, that debtor would be up and out the door! The manager says, "sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) The number goes DOWN, from a hundred to fifty. Half the bill, gone, just like that.

True! "Take your bill and write eighty," he told him. (Luke 16:7) A hundred measures of wheat down to eighty. Not as big a cut as the olive oil man got, but I bet nobody owing that wheat was complaining.

This one's actually true, friend. The second debtor owes a hundred measures of wheat, and then: "Take your bill and write eighty," he told him. (Luke 16:7) The oil went to fifty, the wheat went to eighty. Different numbers, same speedy paperwork.

explanations.answer: He commends him for acting shrewdly
explanations.explanation: He commends him! "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) I was watching through the oven window waiting for smoke, and out comes a compliment. Look close at what gets praised, though. It's the shrewdness, and the verse still calls him the dishonest manager.

explanations.answer: He has him thrown into prison
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a prison, baker. Here's what it says: "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) I was bracing for a cell door too, and instead he gets praised for being shrewd. My eyebrows went so high they nearly knocked my hat off.

explanations.answer: He makes him pay back the difference
explanations.explanation: You'd think so, right? But the text never mentions him paying anything back. "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) Commended, friend! The master praises how shrewd he was, and the same verse keeps calling him dishonest.

It's flipped, friend. The line says "the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) The sons of this age come out ahead on shrewdness here. Easy to swap them, since they're sitting right next to each other in one sentence.

Right, it's the other way around! "For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) The sons of this age win the shrewdness contest. Kind of stings for the sons of light, doesn't it? I felt that one right through my apron.

Eternal dwellings! Jesus says, "use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) Remember that fresh cookie on my counter? The money goes just like that. But notice the word welcome, the same word the manager used about homes (Luke 16:4), and this time the dwellings are eternal.

No royal courts here, friend. Jesus says "they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) The manager was hoping for homes back in his plan (Luke 16:4). Jesus talks about dwellings that are eternal, and that beats any guest list a king could make.

Houses of ivory sound shiny, like that fancy new stamper the Millers brought home. But Jesus says "they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) The wealth is gone, like the cookie off my counter. The dwellings are eternal.

That's the flip Jesus does, and it goes the other way. He says "whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) Dishonest with a little stays dishonest when the stakes get bigger. I wish crooked got straight just by making a bigger batch. Trust me, I tried. MORE crooked cookies.

You got it! Jesus says, "Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) How you handle the little things shows up in the big things. Same way I got my stamp right, one crooked cookie at a time.

True riches! Jesus asks, "So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) He sets worldly wealth right next to true riches and lets you sit with it. Told you that question follows you home and takes the good spot on the couch.
Not a kingdom, baker. Jesus asks, "who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) No crown in this verse. He puts worldly wealth next to true riches, asks His question, and lets it land.

Bigger storehouses would just be more worldly wealth with a bigger roof on it! Jesus asks "who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) Not more of the same stuff. I learned that one the hard way, friend. A bigger drawer just means more room to collect dust.

Another fills the first blank. Jesus asks, "And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) First comes what belongs to somebody else. That was the manager's whole job, looking after the rich man's possessions (Luke 16:1).

Own nails the second blank: "who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) Somebody else's things first, then your own. It's like me holding your cookie box, friend. Hand it back full of crumbs, and see if anybody trusts me with a box of my own.

Strangers is close in spirit, but Jesus keeps it simple: "the belongings of another." (Luke 16:12) Somebody else's things, whoever they belong to. Then He pairs it with "belongings of your own." Theirs and yours, side by side.

Rulers would turn this into a royal story, and Jesus keeps it everyday. He asks about "the belongings of another," (Luke 16:12) just somebody else's things. Then He asks who will give you "belongings of your own." Theirs versus yours, that's the whole contrast.

Family makes it feel close to home, and I love that, but the word is another. Jesus asks about "the belongings of another" and then "belongings of your own." (Luke 16:12) It's not about whose relative owns it. It's about whether it's yours or somebody else's.

explanations.answer: He'll hate one and love the other
explanations.explanation: That's it! "Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) No splitting it down the middle. One of those jerseys is coming off, friend.

explanations.answer: He'll run out of time for both
explanations.explanation: Time isn't what Jesus talks about. He says, "Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) Love and hate, devotion and despising. That's not a crowded calendar, baker. That's picking a side.

explanations.answer: He'll get paid by neither one
explanations.explanation: Jesus never brings up the paycheck. He says the servant "will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) It's loyalty, not payroll. You can't wear both jerseys to the game, no matter who's signing the checks.

No balancing act here, friend. Jesus says it plain: "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) Not "cannot unless you're careful." CANNOT. I tried carrying two cookie trays in two directions once, and I'm still finding crumbs.
Exactly. Jesus says, "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) Not with a schedule, not with a budget, not with a perfect balance. Two masters, and only one gets served.
